chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shummun from Abdillah ibn Abd al-Rahman from Mis'mam from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'The bull-camel (jallatha) — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it is fed for forty days. The bull-cow (jallatha) — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it is fed for twenty days. The bull-sheep (jallatha) — its meat is not to be eaten and its milk is not to be drunk until it is fed for five days. The bull-duck (jallatha) — its meat is not to be eaten until it is tied up for five days. And the rooster [is] three days.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: The Commander of the Faithful, a title referring to Imam Ali (peace be upon him).
key_terms.الْجَلَّالَةُ: A male animal (camel, cow, sheep, etc.) kept in captivity without access to a female, whose meat/milk status is subject to specific waiting periods.
key_terms.تُرْبَطَ: Tied up (referring to the duck, implying confinement to prevent mating or activity).

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating the meat and milk of male animals kept in captivity (Jallatha) according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elaborates on the fiqh of 'Jallatha' (male animals kept in captivity), establishing that their meat and milk are impermissible until the seminal fluids dissipate, a period varying by species to ensure purity. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on ritual purity (taharah) in consumption, linking physical state to spiritual permissibility. The specific durations—forty days for camels, twenty for cows, and five for sheep—demonstrate a nuanced approach to animal husbandry and dietary laws within the Ahl al-Bayt tradition.
